title: Roman telescope passes steady-pointing tests and sees its first stars
summary:
Taking a sharp picture of space requires a very steady telescope. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has now passed important tests of the system that helps it stay pointed at its targets.

From September 15 to 21, engineers tested Roman’s fine-guidance system. It watches guide stars, whose positions are already known accurately. About four times each second, it reports their positions to the system that controls the telescope’s direction. This lets Roman correct tiny movements while collecting light.

The telescope stayed steady to better than one hundred-thousandth of a degree. That is roughly like keeping a laser pointed at a U.S. dime from about 240 kilometers away!

On September 22, Roman’s Coronagraph Instrument received light from space for the first time. A coronagraph reduces a star’s bright light so scientists can study much fainter planets and dusty disks around stars. Even tiny movements could let unwanted starlight spoil an image.

The first test looked at a faint star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighboring galaxy. Its detectors were kept warmer than their final working temperature to help prevent contamination from sticking to them. This made the image noisier.

For a second observation on September 27, engineers cooled the detectors and saw multiple stars. These were early checks of focus and pointing. More complicated tests are still needed before the instrument’s future science observations.
why_it_matters: Steady pointing and focused images help prepare Roman to study faint objects in space.
